How EMI is calculated — the formula explained with real numbers

EMI uses the reducing balance method — you don't pay interest on the full loan amount throughout the tenure. Each month, your EMI splits into two parts: an interest component (charged on the outstanding balance) and a principal component (which reduces the outstanding balance). As the balance drops each month, so does the interest portion — which is why in the amortization table above, early months have high interest and low principal repayment, while later months are the opposite.

The formula: EMI = P × r × (1+r)ⁿ / ((1+r)ⁿ − 1), where P is the loan amount, r is the monthly interest rate (annual rate ÷ 12 ÷ 100), and n is the tenure in months.

Example: ₹10 lakh loan at 8.5% p.a. for 5 years — r = 8.5/12/100 = 0.00708, n = 60. EMI = ₹20,517. Over 60 months you pay ₹12.31 lakh total, meaning ₹2.31 lakh goes as interest — 23% of your loan amount paid purely as interest cost.

The single biggest lever — tenure vs interest rate

Most people focus on interest rate when comparing loans, but tenure has a more dramatic effect on total interest paid. Use the calculator to see this: take a ₹20 lakh home loan at 9% p.a. At 10 years, EMI is ₹25,335 and total interest is ₹10.4 lakh. At 20 years, EMI drops to ₹17,995 — much more affordable — but total interest jumps to ₹23.2 lakh. By extending the loan by 10 years to reduce monthly burden, you pay ₹12.8 lakh extra in interest over the loan's lifetime.

The practical takeaway: take the shortest tenure your monthly budget can comfortably handle. Even 2–3 extra EMIs per year as prepayment can cut years off a 20-year loan and save lakhs in interest.

Current loan interest rates in India (2025)

Home loans: 8.5–9.5% p.a. for salaried borrowers with good credit. SBI, HDFC, and major banks are in this range. Floating rates are linked to repo rate — when RBI cuts rates, floating-rate home loans get cheaper automatically.

Car loans: 8.9–12% p.a. New cars get better rates (8.9–10%) than used cars (11–15%) because the collateral depreciates faster. Manufacturer-tied financing schemes (Maruti, Hyundai) sometimes offer 0% for short tenures — read the fine print, the discount is usually built into the on-road price.

Personal loans: 11–24% p.a. The rate you get depends almost entirely on your credit score and income. A CIBIL score above 750 typically gets you 11–14% from top banks. Below 650, you're looking at 18–24% from NBFCs if you qualify at all. The amortization schedule matters here — on a 24% personal loan, nearly half your early EMIs are pure interest.

Education loans: 9–12% p.a. Government banks (SBI, Bank of Baroda) are cheaper than private. Loans under ₹7.5 lakh don't require collateral. Moratorium period during study means interest accrues but you don't pay EMIs — this capitalises and increases your principal.

How prepayment changes everything

Most home loan lenders allow prepayment without penalty (especially floating rate loans). Even a single lump-sum prepayment of ₹1–2 lakh midway through a loan has an outsized impact because it reduces the outstanding principal, which reduces all future interest calculations. Run the amortization table above to find the month where the outstanding balance crosses a round number you can prepay, then plan around it.

A good rule of thumb: if you receive a bonus, tax refund, or any windfall, putting 50% toward loan prepayment almost always beats putting it in an FD — because the loan interest rate (8.5–24%) typically exceeds FD returns (6–7.5%) after tax.

Frequently asked questions

Why is my actual bank EMI slightly different from this calculator?

Banks may use slightly different rounding conventions — some round the EMI up to the nearest rupee, others to the nearest 10. Some calculate on a 30-day month basis, others on a 365-day year. The difference is usually ₹1–50 per month, not a calculation error. The total interest over the full tenure works out to be nearly identical. If the difference is large (hundreds of rupees), ask your bank to show you their EMI calculation sheet.

What happens if I miss an EMI?

Missing an EMI doesn't just mean a late payment — the unpaid interest gets added to your outstanding principal (this is called penal interest, typically 2% per month over normal interest). For home loans, three consecutive missed EMIs can trigger a loan recall. More immediately, it gets reported to CIBIL within 90 days of default and damages your credit score significantly. If you're expecting cash flow issues, contact your lender for a moratorium before missing — banks have formal restructuring options that don't hit your CIBIL record the same way.

Does EMI change if the interest rate changes (floating rate)?

Yes — when the repo rate changes and your bank adjusts its lending rate, one of two things happens: your EMI amount changes while the tenure stays fixed, or your tenure changes while the EMI stays fixed. Each bank handles this differently. Most Indian banks prefer to extend tenure rather than change EMI when rates rise, which means your loan could run 2–3 years longer than originally planned. Check your loan agreement to know which method your bank uses.

Is it better to take a longer tenure for a lower EMI?

Only if your budget truly requires it. Longer tenure means lower monthly pressure but significantly higher total interest. The right approach: calculate EMI at your target tenure, ensure it's under 40% of your monthly take-home pay (the standard debt-to-income guideline), and if it fits, don't extend the tenure just to have more breathing room. The extra cash flow from a lower EMI rarely gets invested productively — it tends to get absorbed into lifestyle spending.
